facilitatorNotes: The unknown settlement turns, before his eyes, into the farm-house where they started, with their own horses stamping in the barn and dinner on the table. Their desperate plunge has worked better than all their careful plans.
evidence: there stood the farm-house at which we had stopped two days before
had shamed our wisest plans

questions.prompt: In the last paragraph Burroughs says they are both older and younger. Explain the paradox. How might it help explain the essay’s title, “Birch Browsings”?
facilitatorNotes: Older because so much was felt in forty-eight hours that it seems like months or years; younger because the birches gave them “suppleness and strength.” Browsing is how cattle feed on twigs, and also wandering at leisure: the men wandered among the birches and came out nourished, though they caught few fish.
evidence: we were some months, if not years, older at that moment than we had been two days before
for the birches had infused into us some of their own suppleness and strength

readings.title: Birds’-Nests — a farewell walk in the deep woods
readings.challenge: Learn how a naturalist finds what is hidden, and notice where Burroughs’s observations turn into feelings or judgments.
readings.focus: The art of hiding a nest, and the skill of finding one.
readings.context: John Burroughs (1837–1921), an American naturalist who grew up on a farm in the Catskill Mountains of New York, published Wake-Robin, his first book of essays on birds, in 1871; this is its corrected and enlarged edition of 1877. In this essay, Birds’-Nests, Burroughs describes how and where birds build. Primitive woods are untouched forest; consummate means perfect; a fortnight is two weeks; fledged means feathered and nearly ready to fly; perennial means lasting; sylvan means of the woods; pathetic here means touching; twain means two; lichens are crusty growths on bark and rock; a Barkpeeling was a place where hemlocks were cut down and stripped of their bark; Dr. Brewer was an American expert on birds’ eggs; the cow-bunting, now called the cowbird, lays its eggs in other birds’ nests; an interloper is an intruder; potluck is whatever luck brings; an excrescence is a lump; the complement is the full number; incubation is the time eggs are kept warm until they hatch; pendent means hanging.

excerpt.locator: Birds’-Nests, from the nests of the deep woods to the gnatcatcher’s nest; opens “Of course in the deep, primitive woods also are nests; but how rarely we find them! The…”; closes “…that it is much larger, appears almost identical with the nest of the humming-bird.”.

questions.prompt: What is the “simple art” of hiding a nest? How does the black and white warbler’s nest show it?
facilitatorNotes: Using plain, dull materials and placing the nest where it blends with its surroundings. The warbler’s young matched the bark and sticks so well that Burroughs looked twice before he saw them; he found them only because the parent’s alarm gave them away.
evidence: where it blends in color with its surroundings
My eye rested upon them for the second time before I made them out.

questions.prompt: How does Burroughs describe the note of the solitary vireo? Is this science, poetry, or both?
facilitatorNotes: It suggests “the bleating of a tiny lambkin,” and he hears in it “maidenly love,” calling it “love-e.” He also records exact facts about the nest, its fork, lichens and spider-webs. Readers can debate whether the human feelings help us hear the bird or put words in its beak.
evidence: it yet suggested the bleating of a tiny lambkin
It was a rendering into some new sylvan dialect of the human sentiment of maidenly love.

questions.prompt: Why is Burroughs so excited by the mourning ground warbler, and how does he find its nest?
facilitatorNotes: No naturalist had yet seen its nest, “not even Dr. Brewer” the egg expert. After searching inch by inch and fearing to tread on it, he withdraws, waits, comes back and watches exactly where the bird flies from. Patience works where searching failed.
evidence: that not even Dr. Brewer had ever seen the eggs
I bethought me to withdraw to a distance and after some delay return again

questions.prompt: What happens in the red-eyed vireo’s nest? Why does Burroughs call it a “freak of Nature,” and is it fair to judge nature this way?
facilitatorNotes: A cow-bunting’s egg hatches a chick four times the size of the others, smothering them, so the intruder alone thrives. Burroughs reads it as Nature discouraging “prudence and honesty.” Others might say the cowbird is only surviving, and that human virtues do not apply to birds.
evidence: the young interloper was at least four times as large as either of the others
in which she would seem to discourage the homely virtues of prudence and honesty

questions.prompt: Why is the humming-bird’s nest “an event to date from”? Which details of its building and use surprise you?
facilitatorNotes: It is tiny, rare and nearly invisible, like “a mere wart” on a branch. The female builds alone, shaping the cottony nest with her breast, and does not alight on it but “flies into it.” Its rarity puts it next to an eagle’s nest.
evidence: using her breast as a model
The humming-bird, unlike all others, does not alight upon the nest, but flies into it.
